javaMemory.title: Java Memory Model: Primitives, References, Stack & Heap
javaMemory.subtitle: Visualize Thread Stack Frames, Primitive Values, Heap Object Allocations, Pointer References, and Pass-by-Value mechanics.
javaMemory.mentalModel: The Thread Stack manages short-lived method execution frames and primitive local variables. The Heap manages long-lived dynamically allocated objects. Variables on the Stack hold either raw primitive values or reference pointer addresses (@0xADDR) pointing to Heap objects.

failureModes: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError: StackOverflowError occurs when infinite recursion fills up Thread Stack memory. OutOfMemoryError: Java Heap Space occurs when the Heap fills up with unreachable/retained objects faster than Garbage Collection can free them.
tradeOffs: Stack Memory vs Heap Memory: Stack allocation is lightning fast (L1/L2 CPU cache friendly, single pointer movement) but short-lived. Heap allocation supports dynamic lifetimes and thread sharing but incurs Garbage Collection overhead.
theoryData.productionScenario: A production payment service crashed with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java Heap Space`. Thread dump analysis revealed an unbounded static HashMap holding references to User objects, preventing them from becoming Unreachable and blocking Garbage Collection.

interviewQA.a: Java is strictly PASS-BY-VALUE. When passing an object reference to a method, Java passes a COPY of the 64-bit reference pointer address. Modifying object fields affects the shared Heap object, but reassigning the reference inside the method does not change the caller's reference variable.

quizData.question: What happens to local primitive variables declared inside a method when the method finishes executing?
quizData.answer: Their containing Stack Frame is instantly popped and deallocated from CPU stack memory without needing Garbage Collection.

quizData.question: If a method receives `User u` and executes `u = new User("Bob")`, does the caller's `user` variable change?
quizData.answer: NO! Because Java passes a copy of the reference pointer, reassigning `u` only points the local stack copy to a new object on the Heap. The caller's `user` variable still points to the original object.
